inserts.title: Movement and sound share one timeline
paragraphs: Video tracking and acoustic recording capture different sides of the same courtship. Song is identified from the microphone record, and each male's movement is identified from its trajectory. Both streams are kept on one clock, so every sound can be placed at the exact moment of each fly's movement.

Pulse and sine bouts occur at irregular times during the approximately 25 min of courtship. The shared timeline allows the analysis to ask whether a change in movement comes before or after a change in song mode. Each bout is therefore paired with the movement recorded just before it, so the sequence of events can be read in order.

Simultaneous traces also distinguish the male's own motion from the female's motion and from the sound source. Movement-associated noise is therefore kept out of the song measures, and each partner's trajectory is held on its own track throughout the analysis.

inserts.title: Distance alters the balance between song modes
paragraphs: Distance between the two flies changes how much visual information each partner receives. In this experiment, the proportion of pulse song rose as the flies moved farther apart. The effect was measured across several distance bands, which were defined on the same scale for every pair, so each band reflects the same spacing for all pairs.

Darkness changed the mix of song modes, with males tested in the dark producing more pulse song. Both lighting conditions still produced song, so the change lies in the composition of the song rather than in its presence. Both conditions covered the same range of distances, so the lighting change is the main difference between them, and each condition is paired with its own illuminated control.

Visual information therefore takes part in choosing between pulse and sine. Distance and light act on the same song output, so the two cues can be placed in one framework. The framework links each change in song mode to the sensory conditions present at the time it occurred.

inserts.title: Splice alleles isolate the P1 decision
paragraphs: A splice allele changes the sequence that controls one step in RNA processing. Demir and Dickson designed alleles that change the sex-specific P1 splice decision, while other fruitless functions stay intact. Each allele therefore tests one choice in the gene. The wild-type control was run under the same conditions as each allele.

The alleles were verified at the transcript level and at the level of FruM protein in adult brains. A forced female-type allele and a forced male-type allele were checked in the same tissue, so their molecular outputs can be read side by side. Each behavioral result can be linked to a known molecular change in this way.

Because each allele changes one decision, a phenotype can be attributed to that decision. The contrast between the two forced patterns shows which courtship features follow from the male-type splice and which follow from the female-type splice. Each phenotype is therefore traced to a single molecular switch.

inserts.title: Forced male splicing suppresses female egg laying
paragraphs: Receptivity is the willingness of a female to accept mating, and egg laying is a separate reproductive output. Demir and Dickson measured both in females carrying male-spliced alleles, so each female was scored for mating, fertility and egg production together.

Most control females mated within an hour, while fewer than one female in six carrying the male-spliced alleles mated during that time. After mating, control females laid many eggs over three days, whereas the engineered females laid very few. The reduction in egg laying is large and consistent across the females tested.

Behavior, not genital anatomy, carries this reproductive effect, so it is interpreted as a change in what females do. The mating and egg-laying results agree, which makes suppression of female reproductive behavior a coherent outcome of the male splice. The three readouts together describe one reproductive phenotype.

inserts.title: Isoform mutants lose song modes differently
paragraphs: An isoform mutant removes one protein product of the fruitless gene while leaving the others in place. von Philipsborn and colleagues paired each mutant male with a virgin female and recorded pulse song, sine song and copulation, so each mutant is compared on the same measures.

FruC mutants lost sine song and showed the strongest mating impairment among the isoform mutants. Sine song has a carrier frequency of about 120–170 Hz, so its loss removes an entire song mode. FruA and FruB perturbations produced different, milder combinations of defects.

The distinct profiles of the isoform mutants indicate that each isoform contributes a different part of the courtship network. The mutants show that a single gene can influence several outputs through separate protein products. Each isoform's profile is recorded against the same set of measures, so the profiles line up across mutants.

inserts.title: Dark courtship depends on FruC in defined classes
paragraphs: Cell-specific knockdown reduces a gene product only in selected neurons. von Philipsborn and colleagues depleted FruC in defined courtship-related classes and compared pulse production under illumination and in darkness, so each class can be assessed separately.

Knockdown in aSP4 or vAB3 feminized characteristic arbors and impaired courtship in the dark. Pulse amounts measured in light and in darkness divide the visual from the nonvisual contribution. The dark measure isolates the part of courtship that runs without sight. Both light conditions use the same pairing and the same measures.

P1 neuron presence depended on the sex-determination gene doublesex as well as on fruitless. Each neuronal class is assessed for its dependence on both genes, and the combined effects are recorded with the same courtship measures. Those combined results apply across all of the tested classes.

inserts.title: Wing choice is separate from P1 initiation
paragraphs: A population that starts singing and a population that selects a wing can be separate circuits. von Philipsborn and colleagues used stochastic expression to activate P1 neurons on one side or on both sides. Each male's wing choice was recorded against the side of activation, which tests whether the two functions share neurons.

Unilateral activation did not impose a consistent wing choice on the animals. Males chose either wing across repeated bouts and normally avoided extending both wings at once. The wing record therefore stands apart from the side of the activated neurons.

The dissociation places wing selection downstream of, or parallel to, the initiation function. Each bout is scored for its wing, and the activation record and the wing record are kept in the same animals, so the two can be lined up for each male.

inserts.title: vPR6 shortens interpulse intervals with temperature
paragraphs: Interpulse interval is the time between successive pulses in a pulse train. von Philipsborn and colleagues tested whether activation of vPR6 changed this interval, rather than producing an undifferentiated wing movement. Pulse timing is the readout that distinguishes these two outcomes. The interval is measured for each pulse in the train.

Across five genetic patterns, the interval shortened by about 5.4–7.0 ms for each degree of temperature increase. Wild-type intervals changed by about 1.0 ms per degree, so the vPR6 effect is several times larger than the ordinary temperature dependence of song. Each temperature step is plotted on the same baseline.

The effect was associated with patterns containing vPR6 rather than with every song-promoting pattern. Every pattern is plotted on the same scale as the wild-type baseline, which links vPR6 activity to the timing of the pulses. The timing result therefore reflects the vPR6 neurons, not song in general.

inserts.title: GABA knockdown produces bilateral wing extension
paragraphs: Normal courtship usually uses one extended wing at a time. Amin and colleagues knocked down GAD1 or Rdl in fruitless-positive neurons and scored the wing posture of each male. Genetic controls matched the expression system, so the posture change is attributed to the knockdown.

Many knockdown males extended both wings, whereas control males predominantly extended one. The posture defect was scored separately from the timing and waveform of the sound, which kept the motor and acoustic measures distinct.

The result supports an inhibitory contribution to coordinating competing wing movements. Bilateral extension is the defect that inhibition normally prevents, and each male's posture is recorded against its matched control. Bilateral and unilateral posture are contrasted within each genotype.

inserts.title: Brain and nerve-cord GABA affect different outputs
paragraphs: Regional restriction distinguishes a perturbation in the brain from one in the nerve cord. Amin and colleagues confirmed each expression pattern anatomically before scoring behavior, so the region of each effect is known. Each expression pattern is checked before its behavior is measured.

Nerve-cord knockdown reproduced bilateral wing extension and abnormal song. Brain-restricted knockdown did not reproduce those motor defects, and instead impaired courtship conditioning after exposure to an unreceptive mated female. The regional results are all measured against the same conditioning test.

The regional dissociation assigns different inhibitory roles to motor control and to learned changes in courtship. Each role is tied to the region where it was measured, so the two outputs are scored in the same knockdown groups. Each region's output is reported on its own.

inserts.title: Complex bouts follow frontal female positions
paragraphs: Relative bearing describes where the female stands with respect to the male's body axis. Roemschied and colleagues compared bearing, inter-fly distance and bout duration for simple pulse, simple sine and complex bouts, so the geometry of each bout is recorded.

Complex bouts occurred more often when the female was closer and more directly in front of the male. Their duration was longer than that of simple bouts, with distributions spanning about 0 to 3 s. Complex bouts therefore pair a close frontal position with a longer song episode, so position and song duration sit in one record.

Close frontal positions also increase opportunities for contact and change visual motion. The geometry is interpreted alongside those factors, and each bout is described by the female's position at the time it occurred. Each bout's geometry is recorded together with its song.

inserts.title: TN1 neurons show opposing calcium dynamics
paragraphs: Calcium imaging reports changes in intracellular calcium through fluorescence. Roemschied and colleagues combined pIP10 optogenetic stimulation with two-photon imaging in TN1 neurons, so each cell's response is recorded during the same stimulation.

Some TN1 calcium signals tracked the stimulus. Others were anticorrelated and peaked after the stimulus was removed. The recordings kept response timing over several seconds and anatomical positions at a 20 µm scale. Each cell's timing is therefore tied to its position and to the stimulus period.

The opposing dynamics support a functional subdivision within TN1. Each subgroup is defined by its response timing, which places the two groups in different roles in the wing circuit. The subgroups are recorded side by side in the same preparations, so their timing can be lined up directly.

inserts.title: Nested populations share nerve-cord circuitry
paragraphs: A nested activation pattern means that one active population includes another as a subset. Shiozaki and colleagues imaged identified nerve-cord neurons while flies alternated pulse and sine, with wing vibration preserved by attaching parts of the legs. Each neuron is recorded alongside the other recorded classes.

dPR1 signals preferred pulse, whereas TN1A-2 signals remained active during both modes and were stronger during sine. The responses were aligned around transitions on a 0.5 s timescale, so the timing of each change is visible. Each signal's rise and fall is therefore located relative to the moment the song mode switched.

The observations support shared circuit participation with an additional pulse-related population. The pulse and sine populations overlap in a defined way, which is the basis of the nested model. The overlap means that the pulse-related population is contained within the broader population active during song.

inserts.title: pMP2 and pIP10 carry different song dynamics
paragraphs: pMP2 is a descending neuron class that connects the brain and nerve cord. Shiozaki and colleagues recorded its calcium activity alongside pIP10 while flies alternated pulse and sine. Both pathways were imaged on one timeline, so their activity can be placed at the same moment in each song transition.

pIP10 remained active during both song modes. pMP2 was pulse-selective, increasing at sine-to-pulse transitions and declining at pulse-to-sine transitions. Each transition is measured in both pathways on the same 0.5 s scale, which allows the two dynamics to be set side by side.

The two pathways provide differential input to the thoracic network. Each descending pathway contributes according to its own dynamics, and the labeled anatomy identifies which pathway carries each pattern. The pulse-selective pattern therefore comes from a different source than the pattern active in both modes.

2: Courtship song is an acoustic signal that a male Drosophila melanogaster produces by vibrating an extended wing while following a female. Pulse song consists of separated sound pulses, whereas sine song is a relatively continuous, approximately sinusoidal vibration. Both modes come from the same male during one courtship, and each has its own acoustic signature that identifies it in a recording.

Coen and colleagues recorded sound and the positions of both flies at the same time. Their recordings contain transitions between pulse and sine within individual bouts, so the switch between modes happens inside a single courtship event. Typical sine carrier frequencies fall between 120 and 170 Hz, and pulse carrier frequencies fall between 150 and 250 Hz.

**Carrier frequency** describes the oscillations within the sound, whereas the **interpulse interval** is the time separating successive pulses, commonly around 35 ms. These two measures capture different features of the same signal. Measuring both gives a complete description of each song mode, which is why the study reports them together.
3: An acoustic recording identifies sound production, while video tracking identifies the movements that accompany it. Coen and colleagues paired males and females in a small chamber above a microphone array and extracted their trajectories during about 25 min of courtship. Both data streams share one timeline, so each sound can be matched to the positions of the two flies at that moment.

Males sang during roughly 20% of courtship, and they produced many different pulse and sine sequences rather than repeating one stereotyped bout. Simultaneous traces separate male forward motion, female motion and sound. Movement-associated noise is therefore kept apart from the song itself, and the record shows the song choices across the whole courtship.

The preparation allows comparisons between sensory conditions and song choices at short timescales. **Tracking data** show where each fly is at each moment, which makes it possible to link a song choice to the immediate context. Each comparison uses the same chamber and recording setup, so the conditions can be contrasted directly.
4: **Aristae** are the antenna-associated structures removed to disrupt auditory input in this experiment. Cutting a male's wings instead prevents normal wing-generated song. Coen and colleagues compared these manipulations with intact animals, so each effect is measured against a matched control rather than inferred from courtship movements alone.

Deafened females and wing-cut males increased the time to copulation and reduced the fraction of pairs that copulated during the approximately 25 min assay. The male and female manipulations therefore affect different sides of the acoustic interaction. Song reception by the female and song production by the male each contribute to the outcome of courtship.

The outcomes support a contribution of song reception and production to successful courtship. Each surgical manipulation removes one sense or one structure, so a change in courtship success can be linked to that input. Males and females are both tested, which shows which half of the acoustic exchange contributes to success.
5: Sensory history is the sequence of information available before a behavioral event. Coen and colleagues tested whether recent movement predicted song starts and pulse-to-sine transitions, using histories no longer than 600 ms. The short window places the analysis at each song event.

A generalized linear model relates movement features to the probability of a song event. Male forward velocity and lateral speed predicted pulse starts. Forward velocity and inter-fly distance separated pulse from sine starts, so each predictor is weighed alongside the others in the same model.

Increasing male forward velocity and lateral speed favored transitions toward pulse, whereas decreases in forward velocity and increases in female lateral speed favored sine. **Prediction** of each song event therefore follows the movement that precedes it. Each movement feature points toward one song mode or the other, which makes movement patterns a source of information about the next song.
6: **Visual feedback** supplies information about a moving partner's relative position. Coen and colleagues found that the proportion of pulse song increased as the distance between the flies increased, rather than remaining fixed throughout courtship. The change followed the distance between the two animals, and each distance band was measured across the same sessions.

The relationship was evaluated across inter-fly distances of about 3 to 12 mm. Males tested in darkness produced more pulse song than males under illumination, which links the availability of visual information with song composition. Both groups still sang, so the change lies in the mix of song modes rather than in whether the male sings at all.

The finding is consistent with visual signals contributing to the choice between song modes. Darkness changes the interaction in several ways, and the distance records show how partners were positioned in each condition. Visual information therefore counts among the cues that shape song composition, and each lighting condition is paired with its own illuminated control.
7: A female's movement can change the sensory information available to a singing male, while the male's song can influence the female's subsequent movement. Coen and colleagues compared movement and song in paired animals. Courtship is therefore treated as an exchange between two partners, with each partner's behavior tracked on the same timeline rather than as a one-way acoustic broadcast.

Song-related slowing was measured in 1 min windows. Female speed decreased before copulation, and the link between song amount and female speed changed with the paired species and sensory condition. Both D. melanogaster and D. simulans pairs were measured with identical windows, so the species share one time scale.

These observations support a dynamic interaction between partner behavior and song patterning. Correlations across one minute show how the two partners' behaviors change together. Each minute-long window gives the average pattern for that period of courtship, and the shorter analyses on earlier slides address the immediate cause and effect.
8: **RNA splicing** joins selected regions of a precursor RNA to produce a mature transcript. The _fruitless_, or _fru_, locus spans about 130 kb and uses several promoters. Transcripts from promoter P1 undergo sex-specific splicing, so the same gene gives different products in males and females, and the P1 product is the one studied on the following slides.

In males, the default splice pattern produces **FruM**, a male-specific **transcription factor** with a 101-amino-acid amino-terminal extension. A transcription factor regulates gene expression. In females, Transformer-dependent splicing introduces an early stop that prevents production of the full-length FruM protein, so the sex difference starts at the level of RNA processing.

Transcripts from other promoters retain functions shared by both sexes. The sex-specific P1 product is therefore distinguished from the shared transcripts. Each product is identified by its promoter and its splicing pattern, which allows the male-specific form to be tested on its own and makes it possible to ask which courtship functions depend on it.
9: An **allele** is a version of a gene. Demir and Dickson changed the sex-specific splice region while preserving other _fruitless_ functions, which made it possible to test the consequences of the P1 splice decision directly. Each allele was designed to alter only that decision, so the alleles isolate the splice choice from the rest of the gene.

One allele disrupted the male splice donor and forced female-type splicing. A 1601-nucleotide deletion forced male-type splicing, and another allele removed 261 base pairs containing Transformer-binding sites. RNA assays and antibody labeling verified the transcripts and FruM expression in adult brains, confirming that each allele produced the intended product.

Male-spliced alleles produced FruM labeling in females as well as males. The female-spliced allele removed that labeling in males. The verification links each behavioral result to a defined molecular change, so later phenotypes can be traced back to the splice pattern that produced them. Every phenotype is tied to its verified allele, which gives each behavioral result a known molecular cause.
10: Necessity means that removing a factor disrupts an outcome under specified conditions. Demir and Dickson paired males carrying engineered fruitless splice alleles with wild-type virgin females. They measured the proportion of observation time devoted to courtship, using the same pairing and timing for every genotype so that every genotype is measured under identical conditions with the same control.

Males forced into female-type splicing showed very little female-directed courtship, with courtship indices near 80% in control and male-spliced genotypes. Competitive mating assays also separated the female-spliced genotype from males that retained male-type splicing. Both assays point to the same P1 requirement, and each measure gives a separate readout of the same splice change.

The experiment supports a requirement for male P1 splicing in normal male courtship. **FruM** therefore acts during development, so the alleles change courtship across the male's life rather than through a brief command. The timing of this effect is set by when the splice change occurs, and each step in the chain is tied to a verified transcript.
11: **Sufficiency** means that adding or enabling a factor produces an outcome in a defined background. Demir and Dickson tested females engineered to express male-spliced _fruitless_ and paired them with wild-type virgin females to measure female-directed courtship. The same background is used for every comparison, so each genotype is evaluated against controls in the same setting.

These animals performed female-directed courtship with indices above 40%, whereas control females showed essentially none. Wing extension and tapping occurred, although the engineered females did not complete male copulation. The individual components were close to male patterns but not identical to them, so the courtship actions themselves are the outcome being measured.

The result supports developmental sufficiency for many male-typical courtship actions in this genetic background. The set of actions is broad, while copulation is missing, which places the final step outside what the splice change produced. Each action was scored on its own, so the list shows exactly which parts of courtship the splice change can produce.
12: Receptivity is a female's willingness to accept mating. Courtship production and reproductive receptivity are separable behavioral outcomes. Demir and Dickson tested whether forcing male fruitless splicing in females changed mating, fertility and egg laying, in addition to the newly expressed courtship actions. The reproductive measures were scored in the same females, so each female contributes to every readout.

Most control females copulated within 60 min, whereas fewer than 16% of females carrying the male-spliced alleles did so. After mating, control females laid more than 65 eggs over three days on average, while engineered females laid fewer than two eggs. Mating and egg laying are both reduced in the same engineered females.

Behavior, not gross genital anatomy, carries the reproductive phenotype. The findings associate FruM with suppression of female reproductive behaviors. The receptivity and egg-laying results agree, so the phenotype appears as one outcome spanning several measures that reinforce one another.
13: An **isoform** is one of several related protein products of a gene. Male-specific _fruitless_ transcripts can produce **FruA**, **FruB** and **FruC**, which share amino-terminal regions. The three forms differ in their carboxy-terminal zinc-finger domains, which are protein regions involved in binding DNA, so each isoform has its own DNA-binding end.

von Philipsborn and colleagues selectively disrupted these isoforms and compared their effects with controls. The three forms retain a shared BTB domain, which is involved in protein interactions. Their distinct endings provide a molecular basis for different regulatory functions, and the shared domain and the distinct ends are both kept in view.

Sine carrier frequencies normally occupy about 120–170 Hz, and selective isoform disruption produced distinct song phenotypes. These results connect each isoform's protein structure to a particular song outcome. Each isoform is tested against the same song measures, and the phenotypes are then examined by isoform on the next slides.
14: The **ventral nerve cord**, or VNC, contains the thoracic circuitry that controls the wings. Each isoform contributes its own effect in those neurons, and the mutants reveal functions that the overlap would otherwise hide. The same song measures are recorded for every mutant.
15: Isoform-specific mutations distinguish a general requirement for fruitless from a requirement for one of its protein endings. von Philipsborn and colleagues paired mutant males with virgin females and recorded pulse song, sine song and copulation. 16: **Song amount**, **carrier frequency** and **interpulse timing** quantify different outputs of the courtship circuit. von Philipsborn and colleagues measured these parameters separately in selective Fru isoform mutants. 17: A **neuronal arbor** is the branching region through which a neuron receives or distributes signals. von Philipsborn and colleagues labeled identified courtship-related classes and registered their anatomy across male, female and _fruitless_-mutant nervous systems. 20: Synaptic silencing blocks communication from a neuron rather than removing its anatomy. The 2011 study expressed tetanus-toxin light chain in a P1-containing fruitless-positive population. 21: **Laterality** refers to the left–right organization of activity or behavior. Each bout is scored for the wing used, so the side of activation is tracked separately from the activation itself, and both records are compared across the same males.
22: A **descending neuron** sends a process from the brain into the nerve cord. The pIP10 class arborizes in brain regions occupied by courtship-related neurons. 23: **dPR1** neurons occupy the thoracic nerve cord and extend processes into wing-related neuropil. 24: vPR6 identifies a thoracic neuronal class with processes in wing neuropil. von Philipsborn and colleagues used several genetic patterns containing the vPR6-containing neurons. 25: **vMS11** neurons have cell bodies in the mesothoracic nerve cord and processes in wing-related neuropil. 26: **GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an inhibitory neurotransmitter. **GAD1**, glutamic acid decarboxylase, synthesizes GABA. **Rdl** is an ionotropic GABA receptor, meaning that transmitter binding directly controls an ion-channel response. Reducing synthesis limits the available transmitter, while reducing the receptor changes the postsynaptic response to GABA. Both perturbations disrupted courtship motor coordination, so the two manipulations share one motor outcome. The same motor measures score each perturbation, and they are used throughout the following slides.
27: Normal _D. melanogaster_ courtship usually uses one extended wing at a time. Amin and colleagues scored wing posture in males with GAD1 or Rdl knockdown in _fruitless_-positive neurons. Genetic controls distinguish the targeted perturbation from the expression system itself, and posture is recorded for each male in the same way.

Many knockdown males extended both wings, whereas controls predominantly extended one. Control pulse trains were organized around 30–35 ms interpulse intervals. The posture defect is scored separately from the timing and waveform of the sound, so both the posture and the sound are kept as separate measures.

The result supports an inhibitory contribution to the coordination of competing wing movements. Bilateral extension is the defect that inhibition normally prevents. Each male's posture is recorded against its matched control, so the defect appears against a clear baseline, and the contrast between bilateral and unilateral posture is the key measure in both genotypes.
28: A **polycyclic pulse** contains more oscillatory cycles than the usual brief pulse waveform. Every recording is paired with its control, so the genotype difference stays isolated, and waveforms are compared cycle by cycle.

Both measures move in the same direction, and the spread of intervals is the clearest difference.

The defects concern both the organization of successive pulses and the structure of individual pulses. They support a role for inhibition in shaping the motor pattern. Each measure is taken at both the pulse level and the song level, which places the effect at two scales that are described together.
29: The **pulse carrier frequency** measures oscillations within a pulse, while the **sine carrier frequency** measures the continuous vibration of sine song. The two carrier measures are kept separate in every analysis, so each sound is described by its carrier frequencies.

The difference shows that reducing GABA synthesis and reducing one receptor have different consequences across the song. The two perturbations are compared through the same frequency measures, and each is assigned its own frequency profile. Both profiles are shown on the same frequency scale, and the contrast is one of the central results of this study.
30: Regional restriction distinguishes gene perturbation in the brain from perturbation in the nerve cord. The regional dissociation assigns different inhibitory contributions to motor control and to learned changes in courtship. Each contribution is tied to the region where it was measured, so motor control and conditioning are studied as two outputs, each measured against the same knockdown groups.
31: An **acoustic playback** supplies song without requiring the male to produce it. The positive control establishes that the playback could compensate for missing wing-generated sound. Failure in the knockdown males therefore implicates additional courtship motor defects beyond the missing song. Each male's copulation is scored within the playback group it belongs to, and the knockdown result is set against the rescued control.
32: A **simple bout** contains one song mode, whereas a **complex bout** alternates between pulse and sine. Proximity covaries with angle, tapping and other signals, which are examined on the next slide, and each threshold is applied to every bout in the same way.
33: **Relative bearing** describes the female's position with respect to the male's body axis. 34: **Optogenetics** uses a light-sensitive protein to alter neuronal activity. Each delayed sine bout is timed from light offset, so the rebound is measured directly, and sine that follows the stimulus is tied to its cause.
35: A fixed neural stimulation can produce different outputs depending on the animal's context. 36: **TN1** neurons form a heterogeneous thoracic population associated with wing neuropil. 37: **Ih** is a hyperpolarization-activated cation current that can facilitate renewed excitability after inhibition. Hyperpolarization makes the membrane potential more negative. 38: pC2 neurons integrate visual and auditory signals, while P1a is a courtship-related subset of P1 neurons. 39: **Nested activation** means that one active population includes another as a subset. Shiozaki and colleagues imaged identified nerve-cord neurons while flies alternated pulse and sine. 40: Descending input can recruit a shared thoracic population even when the behavioral output is predominantly pulse. 41: A heterogeneous neuronal class can contain subpopulations with different activity preferences. 42: pMP2 is another descending neuron class connecting brain and nerve cord. 43: **Connectomics** reconstructs neurons and their synaptic contacts from electron microscopy. 45: **Genetic background** includes the other genes and regulatory relationships in which a manipulation acts.
